extracted.intended_audience: newspaper editors, publishers, and journalists (newsroom staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical criteria for running and editing a daily newspaper: accuracy, editorial independence, presentation/layout, news selection, newsroom oversight, and staff qualifications as described through J. Pulitzer's practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: "accuracy, accuracy, accuracy!" / "a newspaper should be scrupulously accurate"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated emphasis that the paper must be scrupulously accurate; the author reports that the American press "line for line ... ATTAIN a higher standard of news accuracy" than Europe. The text includes the practice of comparing different versions of the same event over time to test accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to print the news / publicity for democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: "it is the duty of a newspaper to print the news"; publicity exposes secrecy and helps sweep away crime, dodges, tricks, swindles and vices
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that a democracy is advanced by keeping the public informed; newspapers should describe, attack, and ridicule vice so public opinion can remove it. Publicity is framed as essential even if not the only remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decency linked with frankness (avoid salaciousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "a newspaper should be scrupulously accurate, it should be clean, it should avoid everything salacious or suggestive, everything that could offend good taste or lower the moral tone of its readers; but within these limits it is the duty of a newspaper to print the news."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between prudish moral hypocrisy and an appropriate moral tone that combines frankness with decency. Report unpleasant truths, but avoid salacious or needlessly suggestive presentation that offends good taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence from advertisers
rubrics_metrics.description: "If I caught any man on The World suppressing news because one of our advertisers objected to having it printed I would dismiss him immediately; I wouldn't care who he was."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence is a moral and managerial requirement; ties to circulation and advertising revenue are discussed as necessary to secure financial independence (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation and financial independence as necessary for service
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a newspaper is to be of real service to the public it must have a big circulation... second, because circulation means advertising, and advertising means money, and money means independence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulation is justified both as reach (news and comment must reach many people) and as the economic basis for editorial independence. Monitoring circulation/advertising figures is part of oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities required in news, headlines, and editorial page
rubrics_metrics.description: "What a newspaper needs in its news, in its headlines, and on its editorial page is terseness, humor, descriptive power, satire, originality, good literary style, clever condensation, and accuracy, accuracy, accuracy!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A checklist of stylistic and content virtues for copy: brevity, wit, vivid description, satirical edge where appropriate, originality, strong prose style, skillful condensation, all underpinned by accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of sensational/criminal public-interest topics
rubrics_metrics.description: "Some people try and make you believe that a newspaper should not devote its space to long and dramatic accounts of murders, railroad wrecks, fires, lynchings, political corruption, embezzlements, frauds, graft, divorces, what you will. I tell you they are wrong..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit defense of covering dramatic/sensational subjects because they are matters of public interest and secrecy enables wrongdoing. Examples enumerated to justify reportage of such topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article presentation and layout (page/column/space/headlines/type/etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing an item they examined: "On what page was it printed in The World, in what column, how much space did it fill, how much was devoted to headlines, what was the size of the type, was the type varied in parts to give emphasis to the more striking features of the story, what were the cross-heads in the body of the article, were any boxes used, if so, what was put in them, what about the illustrations?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed attention to physical presentation and typographic emphasis as a component of editorial judgment — placement, column choice, headline treatment, type size/variation, cross-heads, boxed material, and illustrations all affect impact and should be scrutinized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom organization and information-collection system
rubrics_metrics.description: An "elaborate organization" collected daily copies of many papers and cuttings, mailed them to J. P. according to cabled instructions; essential matter in each clipping was marked; copies of each issue with writer names were sent for review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic collection, selective clipping, marking essentials for time-efficiency, and sending full issues and bylines to the editor/publisher are prescribed methods for keeping a distant editor informed and able to supervise content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative reading and fact-verification protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading The World first, then other papers covering the same ground, "noting any important differences in the various accounts," mastering in detail about half a dozen articles and comparing treatments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical protocol for verification: read primary paper, then cross-check competing accounts, note discrepancies, and prepare concise notes. This comparative method serves as a check on accuracy and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metrics and classification to monitor content
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports included "an analysis of The Sun, The Herald, The American, The Times, The Tribune and The World, showing the number of columns of advertising, of news, and of special articles, a classification of the telegrams according to geographical distribution... a classification of the special articles on the basis of their topics--medicine, sport, fashions, humor, adventure, children's interests, women's interests."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic statistical reporting and topical/geographic classification of content and telegrams are used as oversight tools to evaluate balance, reach, and topical priorities across competing papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and use of human-interest cuttings for engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: The final reading of the news served to give "from ten to twenty small topics of what Mr. Pulitzer called 'human interest,' to be used as subjects of conversation as occasion demanded" (examples: magistrates' court cases, eccentric entertainments, deaths of centenarians, infant prodigies, museum additions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting and preserving small human-interest items provides material for engagement and conversation; editors/staff should curate such items for topical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for secretaries / staff: loyalty, tact, good temper
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Pulitzer put candidates to a severe test of "ability, tact and good temper" because his blindness and nervous condition required "absolute confidence in the loyalty and intelligence of his companions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hiring and testing procedures should prioritize trustworthiness, discretion, tact under pressure, and steady temperament given the editor's dependence on verbal reports and sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory, observation and accuracy of reporters/secretaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Secretaries were tested on minute descriptions of places and objects (Naples Museum, Acropolis views, Napoleon's villa, etc.) to determine "how much I could see in a given time, and how much of it I could remember with a fair degree of accuracy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong powers of observation and reliable memory are required for staff who must report details orally; training includes directed observation tasks and recall tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stamina and endurance under continuous strain
rubrics_metrics.description: Secretaries were "worked to the limit of their endurance"; duties included constant reading aloud against distractions, long mealtimes requiring sustained attention, preparing a continual stream of information, and being ready for cross-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical expectation that staff will endure long hours, frequent cross-examination, repetitive preparation, and taxing conditions; resilience and tirelessness are workplace criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing noise and protecting noise-sensitive individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Mr. Pulitzer was extremely noise-sensitive, measures included wearing rubber-soled shoes, roping off areas above his bedroom, brass plates on doors warning not to open them when he slept, and eliminating noisy foods/activities; even small sounds could provoke spasms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create procedures and physical controls to minimize incidental noise in the workplace: rules for footwear, restricted access during rest, menu adjustments, and strong norms of quiet behavior to preserve the well-being of sensitive staff or leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensing and preparing literature for a particular audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Two methods to interest Mr. Pulitzer in a novel or play: (1) draw a striking picture of the climax then go back to explain how it came about; or (2) set forth appearance/disposition of characters, condense the narrative to a point and then read from the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting long-form literature to a busy or impatient listener, prepare concise summaries, highlight climactic scenes, or build characters' reality quickly before reading aloud; double preparation (reading the work twice) is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection and amplification of material
rubrics_metrics.description: If any subject "reached the standard of his discrimination he took it up, enlarged upon it, illuminated it, until what had come to him as crude material for conversation assumed a new form, everything unessential rejected, everything essential disclosed in the clear and vigorous English..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial role includes identifying promising material and transforming crude copy by pruning nonessentials and enhancing essential elements to produce clear, vigorous prose.
